transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Corva Coleman.
The massive media merger between Paramount Skydance and Warner Brothers Discovery is
now final.
The combined company Skydance announced the completed acquisition in a statement this
morning.
CEO David Ellison calls it a historic day for the industry.
The $111 billion merger brings together two major film studios, global streaming services
and TV assets, including CBS News and CNN.
The heads of both news networks are staying on board.
The man who killed 13 people in a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas in 2009 will be executed
by firing squad.
NPR's Quill Lawrence reports it's the first military execution in decades.
Nidal Malik Hassan was an Army major stationed at Fort Hood when he opened fire on his fellow
soldiers with a semi-automatic handgun.
32 were wounded and 13 died, including a pregnant soldier.
The Pentagon announced that for the first time since World War II, a firing squad will
be used to carry out Hassan's death sentence.
A military execution requires the President's approval.
Hassan was born in Virginia and became an Army psychiatrist.
He testified at his trial that he carried out the attack because of what he called the illegal
and immoral wars in Iraq and Afghanistan.
Quill Lawrence, NPR News.
Forces in Yemen backed by Saudi Arabia say they've recaptured a port city from Houthi
rebels.
But Houthi rebels based in Yemen are firing into Saudi Arabia.
NPR's Aya Batrawi says Saudi Arabia is now getting help.
To defend against these attacks, Saudi Arabia is getting some support from Britain and France.
Yesterday, top ministers from Pakistan and Turkey also met in Saudi Arabia, and they
confirmed that they're providing rapid military support now to the kingdom as part of the
Mecca agreement.
That's the new defense pact that was signed by the three countries over the summer.
And this pact really stems from President Trump's reluctance to get directly involved
in another war in the Gulf.
The U.S. has not agreed to Saudi Arabia's request for refueling support, but it is sharing
intel on the Houthis.
And Bier's Aya Batrawi reporting.
Two people are dead and nine injured after Ukraine carried out a massive drone attack
on Moscow.
As NPR's Charles Mayne's reports from the city, Ukraine's main target was again energy
facilities.
Moscow mayor Sergei Sabyanin said Russian air defenses destroyed a majority of the 650
drones launched overnight, yet the two fatalities appear to be due to falling debris from intercepts.
And Ukraine successfully targeted the Moscow region's largest fuel storage hub with witness
video showing the facility, which provides oil to the city's main three airports engulfed
in flames.
The attacks follow pledges by Ukrainian President Vladimir Zelensky to continue a months-long
campaign targeting Russian energy infrastructure, a response Zelensky says to Russia's own intensified
airstrikes on Ukrainian cities and heating infrastructure ahead of the winter months.
Charles Mayne's NPR News, Moscow.
This is NPR.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio says the U.S. is closely watching the case of a Russian
lab worker who died last week of the plague.
Russia says the 28-year-old woman died of pneumonia of an unknown origin.
Local officials describe the situation in the area around her lab as stable.
There were unconfirmed Russian media reports.
Several hospitals were under quarantine.
Rubio says Russia must share more information and the U.S. is watching the matter hour by
hour.
President Trump will visit a port just outside Baltimore, Maryland, today.
He's scheduled to speak at an event hosted by defense contractor Endural Industries.
The port is very close to where the Key Bridge collapsed in March 2024.
Six workers were killed.
The Nobel Prize in Physics has gone to a researcher who led an effort to build a giant particle
detector in Antarctica.
NPR's Jeff Brumfield reports.
Francis Halzen has spent his career chasing ghostly particles known as neutrinos.
Neutrinos rarely interact with regular matter, but when they do, they create a tiny flash
of light.
Halzen, at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, developed a plan to place detectors in a cubic
kilometer of ice in Antarctica.
At the time, it seemed like a long shot.
The detector, called Ice Cube, won the prize for finding high-energy neutrinos from deep
space.
Jeff Brumfield, NPR News.
And I'm Corva Coleman, NPR News, from Washington.
Before Bernie Sanders, or AOC, a man named Michael Harrington tried to market socialism
to the American public.
Tens of millions of Americans were poor, miserable, in body and in spirit.
On NPR's Throughline, how the founder of the DSA created a modern political movement, listen
to Throughline in the NPR app or wherever you get your podcasts.

topics.text: Paramount and Skydance complete $111 billion merger, creating major film and streaming company
Nidal Malik Hassan, Fort Hood shooting killer, will be executed by firing squad
Yemen-backed forces recapture port city from Houthi rebels; Saudi Arabia receives military support
Ukraine launches 650-drone attack on Moscow, killing two and targeting energy infrastructure
Secretary of State Rubio monitoring case of Russian lab worker who died of plague
President Trump scheduled to visit port near Baltimore site of 2024 Key Bridge collapse
Francis Halzen wins Nobel Prize in Physics for developing IceCube neutrino detector in Antarctica
